claims.text: Femoral nerve origin: posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2-L4 (lumbar plexus).
claims.quote: The femoral nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2-L4 roots of the lumbar plexus.

claims.text: Femoral nerve course: emerges at the lateral border of psoas, descends between psoas and iliacus (supplying iliacus), then passes under the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle.
claims.quote: The femoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of the psoas muscle at its inferior aspect, before descending between the lateral border of the psoas and the medial border of the iliacus muscles. It sends a motor branch to iliacus before passing under the inguinal ligament to enter the femoral triangle:

claims.text: Femoral nerve supply: motor to the anterior thigh compartment; sensory to the hip, anterior and medial thigh, knee, and medial leg (as the saphenous nerve).
claims.quote: The femoral nerve provides motor supply to the anterior compartment of the thigh and sensory supply to the hip, anterior and medial thigh, knee, and medial leg (as the saphenous nerve).

claims.text: Femoral neuropathy: weak knee extension with numbness over the anterior/medial thigh and medial leg.
claims.quote: Femoral nerve neuropathy results in weakness of knee extension and numbness overlying the anterior/medial thigh and medial leg.

claims.text: Patellar reflex: carried by the femoral nerve (tests L3-L4).
claims.quote: The femoral nerve is responsible for the patellar tendon reflex (tests L3-L4 spinal component).

claims.text: Obturator nerve origin: anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2-4 (lumbar plexus).
claims.quote: Anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2-4 in the lumbar plexus.

claims.text: Obturator nerve course: arises medial to psoas major and descends in the pelvis to the obturator canal, where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
claims.quote: The nerve arises medial to psoas major and descends in the pelvis to the obturator canal where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division exits from the obturator canal to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. The posterior division exits through obturator externus.

claims.text: Obturator nerve supply: anterior division: hip joint, adductor brevis, adductor longus, gracilis and the skin of the mid medial thigh; posterior division: obturator externus and the pubic part of adductor magnus.
claims.quote: Branches of the anterior division include: articular branch to hip joint adductor brevis adductor longus gracilis cutaneous branch: supplies skin along mid-portion of medial thigh Posterior division Branches of the posterior division supply: obturator externus adductor magnus (pubic part)
claims.locator: Gross anatomy: Medial compartment of thigh

claims.text: Obturator nerve injury: weak hip adduction and instability; irritation can cause medial thigh or knee pain.
claims.quote: Injury to the obturator nerve weakens hip adduction and contributes to instability. Irritation of the nerve may result in pain in the medial thigh/knee.

claims.text: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve: a sensory branch of the lumbar plexus (posterior divisions of L2 and L3) to the skin of the anterior and lateral thigh down to the knee.
claims.quote: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, also known as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, is a sensory branch of the lumbar plexus arising from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2 and L3 spinal nerves. The nerve supplies the skin on the anterior and lateral aspects of the thigh to the level of the knee.

claims.text: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve course: passes below (occasionally through) the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, then over sartorius deep to the fascia lata.
claims.quote: The nerve passes below, or occasionally perforates, the inguinal ligament to enter the thigh within a fibrous compartment just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, passing over the sartorius deep to the fascia lata where it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

claims.text: Meralgia paresthetica: compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under the inguinal ligament (or where it pierces the fascia lata) causes lateral thigh pain; decompression may be needed.
claims.quote: meralgia paraesthetica: the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is sometimes compressed as it passes under the inguinal ligament or occasionally where it pierces the fascia lata and may cause pain in the lateral aspect of the thigh; decompression of the nerve may be required

claims.text: Superior gluteal nerve: posterior divisions of L4-S1; leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis, the only nerve to do so.
claims.quote: The superior gluteal nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the L4-S1 nerve roots, along with the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal nerve 1,2. Shortly after forming, it exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen at the most proximal part of the greater sciatic notch 7. It passes above the piriformis muscle through the suprapiriform foramen, the only nerve to do so 1.

claims.text: Superior gluteal nerve supply: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae, plus sensation to the hip joint.
claims.quote: It supplies the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae muscles 1, and provides sensory innervation to the hip joint 2.

claims.text: Superior gluteal nerve injury: most often iatrogenic (highest risk in total hip arthroplasty); hip abductor weakness gives pelvic instability and a Trendelenburg gait. Positive Trendelenburg sign: the opposite side of the pelvis drops when the patient stands on the affected limb.
claims.quote: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve is most often iatrogenic, occurring during arthroscopic and open pelvic surgery, with the highest risk during total hip arthroplasty 2,3. The branch to gluteus minimus is the most vulnerable 2. The resulting weakness of the hip abductors causes pelvic instability and a Trendelenburg gait. A positive Trendelenburg sign is drooping of the contralateral pelvis when the patient stands on the affected limb 2.

claims.text: Sciatic nerve: from the sacral plexus (L4-S3); the longest and widest single nerve in the body.
claims.quote: The sciatic nerve arises from the sacral plexus from the roots of L4-S3 and runs through the buttock and down the lower limb. It is the longest and widest single nerve in the body.

claims.text: Sciatic nerve components: tibial part from the anterior divisions of L4-S3; common peroneal part from the posterior divisions of L4-S2.
claims.quote: The nerve forms from the anterior divisions of the L4-S3 roots (which form the tibial component) and posterior divisions of the L4-S2 roots (which form the common peroneal component) of the sacral plexus.

claims.text: Sciatic nerve course: leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, descends midway between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity through the posterior thigh, and divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common peroneal nerves.
claims.quote: The sciatic nerve enters the lower limb by exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, below the piriformis muscle and above the superior gemellus muscle. It descends midway in between the greater trochanter of the femur and the tuberosity of the ischium and in the posterior compartment of the thigh to the apex of the popliteal fossa, where it divides into two large terminal branches: tibial nerve common peroneal nerve

claims.text: Sciatic nerve muscles: long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus and adductor magnus from the tibial part; short head of biceps femoris from the common peroneal part.
claims.quote: biceps femoris: supply to short head arises from the common peroneal part, supply to long head arises from the tibial part semitendinosus: arises from the tibial part semimembranosus: arises from the tibial part adductor magnus: arises from the tibial part

claims.text: Sciatic nerve sensation: none directly; through its branches it supplies the sole (tibial), the dorsum of the foot (common peroneal) and the leg except its inner side (saphenous nerve).
claims.quote: sensory supply: no direct sensory function. Indirect sensory supply to the foot (plantar surface: tibial nerve, dorsal surface: common peroneal nerve) and the leg (except its inner side, which is supplied by the saphenous nerve)

claims.text: Causes of sciatic pain: compression or irritation from disc herniation, degenerative disc disease, spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis or piriformis syndrome.
claims.quote: Pain and functional symptoms may be caused by a compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve. This may be caused by: spinal disc herniation degenerative disc disease spinal stenosis spondylolisthesis piriformis syndrome

claims.text: Tibial nerve origin: anterior divisions of L4 to S3 (tibial part of the sciatic), separating from the sciatic nerve usually in the lower third of the thigh.
claims.quote: Fibers arise from the anterior divisions of the L4 to S3 nerve roots in the sacral plexus to form the tibial component of the sciatic nerve. It forms its own discrete nerve after the terminal division of the sciatic nerve, usually in the lower third of the thigh.

claims.text: Tibial nerve course: straight down the popliteal fossa behind the popliteal vessels, between the heads of gastrocnemius and deep to soleus; at the ankle it passes under the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel and divides at the medial malleolus into the medial and lateral plantar nerves and the medial calcaneal nerve.
claims.quote: Passes straight down through the popliteal fossa, posterior to the popliteal vessels, to pass inferiorly between the heads of gastrocnemius and deep to the soleus muscle. In the posterior calf, it continues inferiorly in the midline, deep to the soleus and superficial to the tibialis posterior muscles. At the ankle, it passes under the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel, enclosed in a synovial sheath containing the posterior tibial vessels. At the level of the medial malleolus it divides into three terminal branches: medial and lateral plantar nerves, and the medial calcaneal nerve.

claims.text: Tibial nerve supply: motor to the posterior thigh, the superficial and deep posterior leg compartments and the sole of the foot; sensory to the knee, ankle and foot joints, posterior calf and sole.
claims.quote: motor supply: posterior compartment of the thigh, posterior compartments of the leg (superficial posterior and deep posterior) and the muscles of the sole of the foot sensory supply: articular branches to knee, ankle and foot joints; cutaneous branches to posterior calf and sole of the foot

claims.text: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve origin: terminal branch of the sciatic nerve, usually separating in the lower third of the thigh; posterior divisions of L4-S2.
claims.quote: One of two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve, with the division typically occurring in the lower third of the thigh. It arises from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L4-S2 nerve roots in the sacral plexus.

claims.text: Common peroneal nerve course: runs laterally in the popliteal fossa medial to biceps femoris, winds around the neck of the fibula (where it can be felt and rolled) into the lateral compartment, and divides in peroneus longus into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves.
claims.quote: Diverges away from the sciatic nerve by sloping laterally and downwards to lie laterally in the popliteal fossa, medial to the biceps femoris muscle. It exits the popliteal fossa over the plantaris muscle and lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle. Here, the common peroneal nerve remains subfascial as it winds its way around the neck of the fibula to enter the lateral compartment of the leg, where it can be felt and rolled in the living. It divides into its terminal branches, the superficial and deep peroneal nerves, in the peroneus longus muscle.

claims.text: Peroneal branches: deep peroneal nerve → extensor (anterior) compartment muscles and the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes; superficial peroneal nerve → lateral compartment muscles and the skin of the dorsum of the foot.
claims.quote: superficial peroneal nerve: medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves supply the skin on the dorsum of the foot deep peroneal nerve the terminal branch gives off the dorsal digital nerve to supply adjacent sides of the 1st and 2nd toes peroneal communicating branch joins the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve) to form the sural nerve that supplies the posterolateral side of the leg and the dorsolateral aspect of the foot motor supply deep peroneal nerve: muscles of the extensor compartment of the leg superficial peroneal nerve: muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg

claims.text: Peroneal palsy risk: compression against the fibular neck is most common in emaciated bedbound patients and thin people who habitually cross their legs.
claims.quote: Peroneal nerve palsy is usually caused by compression of the nerve against the lateral aspect of the fibular neck. It is most common among emaciated bedbound patients and thin people who habitually cross their legs.
